nameStory: This fern gets its name from the Green Mountains of Vermont, where it was first discovered as a distinct species in 1991. The scientific name 'viridimontanum' literally means 'green mountain' in Latin, honoring the Vermont peaks where botanists realized this wasn't just another western maidenhair fern, but something special all its own.
description: Green Mountain maidenhair fern is a delicate, rare fern that grows only on rocky serpentine outcrops in New England and eastern Canada. Its fronds are divided into graceful finger-like segments that spread from a curved, dark stem like an open hand. The individual 'fingers' can either droop elegantly in shady spots or stand more upright in sunny locations. This is one of New England's rarest ferns, with only 33 recorded sightings across the region.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively on thin, exposed serpentine rock outcrops - a greenish, often slippery-feeling rock type that's toxic to many plants

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Leaves divided into finger-like segments that radiate from a curved, dark glossy stem, resembling an open fan or hand

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Dark, glossy, curved stem that feels smooth to the touch and creates the characteristic arched shape of the frond

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Finger segments may droop gracefully in shade or stand more erect in sunny exposures, giving the same plant different postures

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spores hidden under false covers (indusia) along the edges of the smallest leaf divisions, creating tiny brown dots at the margins

habitat: This extremely rare fern grows only on outcrops of serpentine rock, a distinctive greenish rock type found in scattered locations across New England. You'll find it clinging to thin soils on these exposed rocky sites, quite different from the rich woodland habitats preferred by most other ferns. Look for it in the Green Mountains of Vermont, parts of Quebec, and one known coastal site in Maine.

seasonality.spring: New fiddleheads emerge from the rock crevices, unfurling into the characteristic finger-like fronds as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Fronds reach full size and begin producing spores along their margins. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive serpentine habitat is most obvious.
seasonality.fall: Spore production continues and fronds begin to show wear from the harsh growing conditions on exposed rock.
seasonality.winter: Fronds die back, leaving only the underground portions alive in the protected rock crevices until spring returns.

funFact: This fern is actually a hybrid species - a natural cross between two other maidenhair ferns that was hiding in plain sight for decades until a sharp-eyed botanist realized these weren't quite like any other fern she'd seen before!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from western maidenhair fern without close examination, but the habitat is the giveaway - Green Mountain maidenhair grows only on serpentine rock, while western maidenhair prefers rich woodland soil. Remember: serpentine site = special species.
contextualKnowledge: Until 1991, botanists thought this was just the western maidenhair fern growing in odd eastern locations. It took years of careful study to realize these serpentine-loving plants were actually a distinct hybrid species, showing how much we're still learning about our local flora.
compareHints: Green Mountain maidenhair is extremely difficult to separate from western maidenhair fern without magnification, but habitat tells the story - it grows exclusively on serpentine rock rather than rich woodland soil. Compared to the more common northern maidenhair fern, it has the same finger-like frond pattern but grows in harsh rocky sites rather than shaded forest floors, and the individual leaflet shapes are subtly different under close inspection.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern maidenhair fern is much more common in New England than its rare cousin, Green Mountain maidenhair fern, which is found only in a few spots in Vermont.

Western maidenhair differs from northern maidenhair fern by its more openly branched fronds that spread in multiple directions, while northern maidenhair creates a distinctive horseshoe-shaped arrangement.
